score_meanings.promise_vocabulary: 0 drifts into claims/profiles/central trust-ledger framing, 5 stays promise-first and pCID-specific
score_meanings.simplicity_durability: 0 overbuilt or fragile, 5 minimal, durable, and small-device-friendly under the 100-year goal

promise_theory_rules: A promise is a scoped declaration of intent.
No agent can make a promise on behalf of another agent.
Trust is a local assessment of whether a promise will be kept.
Promises to receive or use are not equivalent to obligations, impositions, or promises to give.
promise_theory_references: Mark Burgess, In Search of Certainty
Mark Burgess, Promise Theory: Principles and Applications

assessment.rationale: The design partially fits relationship-scoped adoption because session-local conditions can vary by conversational context, but it targets conditional release more than adoption metadata. Its promise framing is mixed: participants promise their own forwarding behavior, yet the session layer also carries policy-like conditions that can look normative and blur layer boundaries.
strengths: Supports context-local variation rather than forcing one peer-wide rule.
Implementation is plausible with message-carried or referenced conditions.
Keeps some agency at the participant level for onward dispatch decisions.
weaknesses: Not directly about adoption metadata, so scenario fit is only moderate.
Layer boundary between session transport and policy/promise semantics is unclear.
Failure and violation handling are underspecified.
Promise vocabulary is weaker than a payload-first explicit promise card or assertion.
risks: Relationship-specific behavior may be encoded indirectly through session policy instead of explicit peer-local adoption promises.
Auditors may not be able to distinguish a kept promise from merely propagated condition text.
Bundling release policy into session semantics may make long-term evolution and interop brittle.
open_questions: Can session-local release conditions cleanly express Bob using one relationship profile with Alice and another with Carol without looking like peer-wide inconsistency?
What local audit artifact shows that a participant accepted a conditional-release promise versus merely received content with attached policy text?
How are refusal, stripping, or reinterpretation of release conditions by later recipients represented without implying guaranteed enforcement?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; does not settle PromiseGrid design.

autonomous_agents.note: Participants are described as making their own onward-restraint promises; no central actor is required.

scoped_intent.note: Intent is scoped to a group/session and later dispatch actions, which is narrower than peer-global identity claims.

no_promises_for_others.note: The design mostly keeps promises attached to each participant's own dispatch behavior.

no_guaranteed_outcomes.note: Participants can promise their own forwarding behavior, but the design does not guarantee downstream compliance.

local_trust_assessment.note: Trust can remain peer-local, but session-embedded policy may encourage a shared/global reading of compliance.

accept_use_not_obligation.note: Carrying release conditions inside session semantics risks treating receipt or forwarding as an obligation rather than a voluntary promise.

violations: Session-carried release conditions can be read as imposed obligations on recipients rather than explicit voluntary promises.
Embedding onward-restraint in group/session semantics blurs local trust assessment and weakens clear promise-layer boundaries.
